result:
Before diving into the math — there's a premise here worth stopping on.

Your makerspace assistant won't be *trained* by you at all. It'll call an already-trained model (the kind you've been learning to call in a loop, with tools) through an API. The heavy RL work — PPO or similar — already happened at the company that built that model, on far more compute and data than a sponsor's small budget or a five-week timeline could ever cover. Your team's job is to prompt it well and design good tools, not to run a training loop. This is actually spelled out in your own `MISSION.md`, under "Out of scope": *"Training or fine-tuning models, and the math inside them."* That line exists because training doesn't move the needle on what you're building — tool design and architecture do.

So, honestly and briefly, here's what PPO *is*, without the derivation: it's an RL algorithm where the model produces an output (a sentence, a tool call), a reward signal says how good that output was, and the algorithm nudges the model's parameters to make good outputs more likely. The "proximal" part caps how big each nudge can be, so one update doesn't wreck everything the model already learned. That's the honest shape of it — the actual objective (the clipped surrogate loss, advantage estimates, KL terms) is the math your mission rules out, and it wouldn't change a single decision you make for your assistant.

What *would* help your tool-calling, concretely: the quality of a tool's name, description and parameter schema is most of what makes a model call it correctly — that's your mission's own success criterion #2. Want a lesson on writing a tool description that a model calls reliably, with a worked example from your booking-calendar tool? That's the lever you actually control.

Quick check: can you say in one sentence why retraining a model isn't the thing your team would do to get better tool calls?
